one_liner: Header-only C++20 enum-to-string and string-to-enum for bounded enums, with 16-183x less instantiation time than magic_enum's default-range enum_name.
what_it_does: Gives enum_name(value) returning std::string_view, enum_cast<E>(std::string_view) returning expected<E, enum_cast_error>, enum_index, a ranges-compatible enum_view, an enum-indexed bitfield, and std::format, fmt, glaze JSON and std::error_code integrations. You declare each enum's bounds in one of three ways: first/last enumerators inside the enum, a consteval adl_enum_bounds(E) function found by ADL that returns simple_enum::adl_info{first, last}, or a simple_enum::info<E> specialization for enums you cannot edit. Enums without bounds fall back to the range [0, default_unbounded_upper_range], which is 10 by default and can be overridden with a macro. The call syntax resembles magic_enum, but the namespace, return types and bounds requirement differ.
how_it_is_fast: It uses the same __PRETTY_FUNCTION__/__FUNCSIG__ trick as magic_enum: it instantiates se::f<value>() and parses the enumerator name out of the signature string. It does this only for the values in the declared [first, last] range, so the work grows with the range width. magic_enum 0.9.5's default scan covers [-128, 127], clamped to 0-127 for a uint8_t enum. Only the first value scans for the qualified-name prefix (first_pass). Every later value starts at that saved offset and only searches for the closing ']' (cont_pass). Hard-coded per-compiler offsets and a one-letter namespace (se) keep the strings short. The result is a constexpr array of (pointer, length) pairs, so a runtime enum_name is a range check plus an array index. enum_cast runs a lower-bound search over an index array that is sorted at compile time, using a binary/linear hybrid tuned for about 256 entries.
when_to_use: Codebases with many enums where magic_enum's compile time is a measurable cost and you can annotate each enum with first/last or an adl_enum_bounds function.
Dense, contiguous enums of any size: the README measures a 104-enumerator enum at about 12 ms of instantiation time, against about 200 ms for magic_enum at its default range.
Enums whose values lie far outside [-128, 127], for example the README's adl_enum_bounds example starting at -15345953: only the width of the range matters, not where it starts.
Third-party enums you cannot modify (the info<> specialization, e.g. std::memory_order).
Projects that already use glaze JSON, std::format or fmt and want enum names in serialization and formatting without hand-written tables.
when_not_to_use: Sparse enums with a wide range: each value between first and last instantiates one se::f<value>(), so an enum spanning 0 to 1,000,000 is impractical. Holes cost compile time and come back as empty names.

Enums you will not annotate: the unbounded default covers only 0 to 10, values outside it silently give an empty string_view, and issue #34 reports conversion warnings for an 8-value enum because the library casts 8 and 9 into it.
Flag/bitmask enums: the README still lists 'enum bitmasks support' as planned, unlike magic_enum's flags mode.
C++17 projects, or builds with CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD below 23: the headers need C++20, and the top-level CMakeLists.txt stops with a FATAL_ERROR 'Minimum required standard is C++23'.

Toolchains with C++26 static reflection: magic_enum's current docs say it switches to standard reflection automatically there, so the 2024 comparison against magic_enum's __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ scan may no longer hold.

integration.form: header-only (an optional C++ module build produces a static library)
integration.dependencies: none for the core (standard library only); glaze, fmt optional for those integrations
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 for the headers (README), GCC 10+ or Clang 13+ enforced by #error checks, MSVC tested; the repo's own CMake build requires C++23 and CMake 3.28
integration.platforms: any target, but only on GCC, Clang or MSVC (relies on their __PRETTY_FUNCTION__/__FUNCSIG__ layouts; other compilers hit #error)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; enum_name and enum_cast are noexcept and read only constexpr static tables
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: enum_name(value) has the same call shape as magic_enum::enum_name, but the namespace differs, enum_cast returns expected<E, enum_cast_error>, and enums outside 0-10 need declared bounds

gotchas: enum_name returns a string_view into the compiler's __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ string, ending before the ']' and not null-terminated, so do not pass .data() to C APIs. The tables point into one full signature string per value in the range.

Bug fixes landed on 2026-10-01 after the v0.9.5 release commit (PR #39): before them, the first hole in a sparse range was named "0", enum_cast("0") or enum_cast("") could match an invalid entry, and an index-to-enum lookup narrowed the index before the range check (an int8 index of 200 became -56 and was accepted). Use master after that date or a later tag.

Benchmark harness flaw: simple_enum runs with exact bounds, but magic_enum runs at its default range: 256 values for the int-based enums and 128 for the uint8_t enum E, which explains E's lower 86 ms. An equal-range magic_enum run (customize::enum_range) is not measured. Each library's four per-enum figures come from one translation unit with a different call order (simple_enum.cc calls lorem_ipsum_long first, magic_enum.cc calls E first), so shared one-time instantiation cost falls on different rows.

The table cannot be reproduced from the repo at HEAD: time_trace/CMakeLists.txt links magic_enum::magic_enum and reflect::reflect, but no CMake file fetches them, no file adds -ftime-trace, and SIMPLE_ENUM_ENABLE_TIME_TRACE is not a declared option. The magic_enum_enum_cast_tt target links only simple_enum.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No enum-reflection library is catalogued in this category yet; the siblings (Cista++, struct_pack, YAS, bitsery, FBE and others) are serializers. Use simple_enum alongside them when you need enum/string conversion for those formats; it ships glaze integration, and compile time matters more than flag-enum support.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README table for simple_enum v0.2.0 (2024), measured with clang 17 -ftime-trace on an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X running Gentoo Linux. It reports the template instantiation time of one enum_name call per enum: 12.2 vs 199.9 ms against magic_enum 0.9.5 for 104 enumerators, 5.3 vs 178.9 ms for 40, 2.6 vs 86.1 ms for 16 (labelled 15), and 0.83 vs 151.6 ms for 3. reflect (main of 2024-02-02) totals 46 to 69 ms including code generation. These are compile-time figures only, magic_enum ran at its default range, and there is no runtime benchmark.
status_note: Active single-maintainer project (44 stars, v0.9.5, bug-fix and clang 23 CI commits on 2026-10-01), BSL-1.0 and header-only so easy to vendor, but the performance table dates from v0.2.0 and has not been regenerated.
